answers.explanation: Bits come off the wire (layer 1), the frame is checked and stripped (layer 2), then the IP destination is looked up (layer 3).
That's the classic way IP forwards. (Some routers can also match on other fields, which SDN generalizes later in this chapter.)
If lookup is slower than line rate, packets pile up in the input queue.
A crossbar has separate paths between each input and each output. Memory and bus fabrics move one packet at a time.
The bus is shared. Copying each packet twice through memory is the memory fabric's limit.
Each output can only take one packet at a time. That conflict is what causes head-of-line blocking.
That's head-of-line blocking: the front of the queue holds up everything behind it.
That's why they were slow: every packet crossed the memory bus twice.
